As-built notes: LAN gateways remain .5. Wazuh was rebuilt on Ubuntu 24.04 and includes its Indexer; the internal indexing path was retained. The actual Shuffle hostname is soc-soar-shfl. Disk values are configured capacities, not consumed SSD space. Only Pod A is routinely powered on; other VMs are enabled for each task. See hardware budget. The management endpoint remains planned.

docs.title: 2.3 Data Flow Design
docs.text: Attack traffic path: Kali (10.10.30.10) → pfSense → Windows victim (10.10.20.20) Detection path: Windows victim (Wazuh agent) + pfSense (IDS) → logs forwarded → SIEM (10.10.10.10) Validated response path: Windows Application event → Wazuh manager → Shuffle webhook → marker condition → Wazuh API → agent 001 → marker file. Reversal is a separate manually started Shuffle workflow. ELK and Splunk remain parallel ingestion destinations; neither SIEM triggers this playbook.

docs.title: 2.4 Naming Convention
docs.text: Use a consistent prefix so VMs are easy to identify in VMware's library: SOC-<role>-<os>, e.g. SOC-FW-pfSense, SOC-SIEM-ELK, SOC-Vict-Win10, SOC-atk-Kali, SOC-ADSRV-Win19, SOC-XDR-Wazuh, SOC-Vuln-OpenVAS — see the inventory table in 2.2 for the full current list.

docs.title: Exit Criteria for Phase 2
docs.text:
• [ ] Network diagram (zones + subnets) written down
  • [ ] IP address table completed
  • [ ] Naming convention chosen

docs.title: PHASE 3 — Implementation (Build)
docs.text:
Goal: Build the lab in a strict order — network first, then infrastructure, then detection tools, then the attacker.

Build one item at a time. Fully finish and confirm each step works before starting the next — this is the core discipline of Waterfall.

docs.title: Step 3.1 — Prep VMware Workstation
docs.text:
1. Open VMware Workstation Pro → Edit → Virtual Network Editor.
  2. Create/confirm 3 Host-only networks (VMnet1, 2, 3) matching the subnets in 2.2. Untick "Use local DHCP service" for each — pfSense will hand out addresses instead, just like a real firewall.
  3. Leave VMnet8 (NAT) as-is for pfSense's WAN.

docs.title: Step 3.2 — pfSense (build this first — everything else depends on it)
docs.text:
1. Download pfSense CE ISO (free) from the official pfSense site.
  2. Create VM: 2GB RAM, 2 vCPU, 80GB thin-provisioned disk, 4 network adapters (WAN=NAT, LAN1=Mgmt, LAN2=Corp, LAN3=Attacker).
  3. Install pfSense, assign interfaces to match Section 2.1.
  4. From a browser on the host, log into pfSense's web interface and set up firewall rules: allow Management zone to reach everything (you need visibility everywhere); restrict Attacker zone to only reach Corp zone (simulates an external attacker reaching internal systems, not admin tools).
  5. Confirm: ping between zones behaves as designed before moving on.

5a. Confirm outbound internet access (needed for Windows Updates, apt update, tool downloads on every VM):

  • Host-only networks are not internet-isolated by default — pfSense routes and NATs each LAN's traffic out through its WAN interface (which rides VMware's NAT network, VMnet8, out to your host's real connection) the same way a real office's internal network reaches the internet only through its edge firewall.
  • Check Firewall → NAT → Outbound is set to "Automatic" — this makes pfSense NAT traffic from all three Host-only subnets out to WAN with no extra config.
  • Set each VM's DNS server to its pfSense LAN IP (10.10.10.5 / 10.10.20.5 / 10.10.30.5), and confirm pfSense's DNS Resolver is enabled (Services → DNS Resolver) — default install has this on, but confirm it. No working DNS means updates will silently fail even with a good route.
  • Temporarily allow outbound traffic while building/patching: while you're actively installing OS updates or tools on a new VM, add a permissive "allow any outbound" rule on that VM's zone so nothing blocks the install. Remove or tighten it once the VM is fully built and patched — see the hardening step in Phase 5.
  • Confirm: from each VM, browse a website or run a package update and verify it completes successfully before moving to the next VM build.

docs.title: Step 3.3 — Corporate LAN victims
docs.text:
1. Build Windows Server VM (4GB/2vCPU/60GB), install, promote to a Domain Controller (this makes it the "brain" of a mini corporate network with user accounts — a standard SOC training setup).
  2. Build Windows 10/11 victim VM (4GB/2vCPU/60GB), join it to the domain.
  3. Assign static IPs per Section 2.2.

docs.title: Step 3.4 — Wazuh (HIDS/XDR)
docs.text:
1. Build a Wazuh manager VM on Ubuntu 24.04 (6GB/4vCPU/100GB), using Wazuh's official install script. Decision made: the official Wazuh OVA was tried first and abandoned after integration difficulties (different base OS from the rest of the lab caused several build steps to assume the wrong package manager, and its bundled Filebeat conflicted with the log-forwarding setup) — see Configure Log Forwarding for the full story. Building from scratch on the same Ubuntu base as everything else removed that whole class of problem.
  2. Install the Wazuh agent on the Windows victim VM and point it at the manager.
  3. Confirm: Wazuh dashboard shows the Windows agent as "active."

docs.title: Step 3.5 — IDS (Suricata)
docs.text:
Decision made: installed as a pfSense package rather than a standalone VM, for simplicity — one less VM to build, patch, and keep running.

  1. ~~Enable Suricata as a pfSense package~~ Done.
  2. Point it at the Corp-zone interface so it inspects traffic to/from your victim machines.

docs.title: Step 3.6 — SIEM #1: ELK Stack
docs.text:
Full step-by-step build guide: Build Guide: ELK Stack VM

  1. Build ELK VM on Ubuntu 24.04 (actual: 8GB RAM / 4 vCPU / 100GB disk), static IP 10.10.10.10.
  2. Install Elasticsearch, Kibana, and Logstash.
  3. Configure Logstash/Beats to receive logs from Wazuh, pfSense, Suricata, OpenVAS, and Windows — see ELK Ingestion Plan for objectives/sequencing/exit gates, or jump straight to Configure Log Forwarding for the commands. Deliberately split out as its own step: it touches five separate VMs, not just this one, and is easy to defer until both SIEMs and OpenVAS exist and you can wire up everything at once.
  4. Confirm: logs appear in Kibana within a few minutes of test traffic.

docs.title: Step 3.7 — SIEM #2: Splunk Enterprise
docs.text:
Full step-by-step build guide: Build Guide: Splunk Enterprise VM

  1. Build Splunk VM (6GB/2vCPU/100GB), static IP 10.10.10.14.
  2. Install Splunk Enterprise via the free trial license (fine for a lab, not for production).
  3. Configure the same log sources as ELK — see Configure Log Forwarding, so you can compare how each SIEM presents the same data — this is a genuinely useful comparison exercise for interviews.
  4. RAM note: Pod A is 12GB; adding ELK and Splunk totals 26GB. Power receivers on as needed and leave Shuffle/OpenVAS off for dual-SIEM sessions.

docs.title: Step 3.8 — OpenVAS (Vulnerability Management)
docs.text:
Full step-by-step build guide: Build Guide: OpenVAS (Greenbone Community Edition)

  1. Build OpenVAS/Greenbone VM on Ubuntu 24.04 (actual: 6GB RAM / 2vCPU / 100GB), static IP 10.10.10.12 — Docker-based install, using Greenbone's official Community Edition container stack.
  2. Point a scan at the Windows victim VM's IP.
  3. Confirm: a vulnerability report generates.
  4. RAM note: this is the tightest fit yet with two SIEMs already running — see the guide's "Before you start" section.

docs.title: Step 3.9 — SOAR
docs.text:
Status: complete for the agreed controlled response and manual reversal scope, September 22, 2026.

As-built record: Shuffle Deployment and Response Validation.

  1. Deployed Shuffle on soc-soar-shfl, 10.10.10.13, Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, 8GB RAM / 4 vCPU / approximately 100GB disk.
  2. Verified Docker, Compose, admin login, workflow execution, and a successful workflow run after reboot.
  3. Configured Wazuh's native Shuffle integration for JSON alerts at level 7 or higher; retained both syslog outputs and Indexer.
  4. Validated Windows rule 60602 (level 9), matching payload IDs across Wazuh and Shuffle.
  5. Tested positive and negative marker conditions between app actions.
  6. Created API account shuffle_lab, linked to role shuffle_lab_operator and policy shuffle_lab_response, scoped to agent 001.
  7. Automatically created a marker file via the Wazuh API and confirmed its contents on Windows.
  8. Removed that marker via a separate manual Shuffle reversal workflow and confirmed Test-Path returned False.

TheHive/Cortex remain deferred. This is a marker-file demonstration, not host isolation, AD account disabling, or completion of Phase 4's attack tests.

docs.title: Step 3.10 — Kali (Attacker)
docs.text:
1. Kali is built (4GB/4vCPU/40GB); keep it on the Attacker Zone network only.
  2. Power it on only for the selected attack exercise after checking the network rules.

docs.title: Exit Criteria for Phase 3
docs.text:
• [ ] Every VM listed above is built and powered on successfully at least once
  • [ ] pfSense routes and filters traffic between all zones as designed
  • [x] Wazuh shows an active agent
  • [x] At least one SIEM is receiving logs
  • [x] OpenVAS has completed one scan
  • [x] SOAR has one working playbook

Phase 3 has not been blanket-signed off: confirm the inventory-wide power-on checklist and network filtering separately. Step 3.9 does not close the Phase 4 attack matrix.

docs.title: PHASE 4 — Testing & Verification
docs.text:
Goal: Prove the lab actually detects and responds to attacks, end-to-end.

Test Steps Pass condition Network isolation From Kali, try to reach the Management zone directly Blocked by pfSense Attack detection (network) Run an Nmap scan from Kali against the Windows victim Suricata logs the scan Attack detection (host) Run a brute-force login attempt against the Windows victim Wazuh raises an alert SIEM ingestion Check Kibana/Splunk during the above tests Wazuh + Suricata events visible within minutes Vulnerability scan Run OpenVAS against the victim Report lists real findings (e.g., missing patches) SOAR response Trigger the alert type your playbook watches for Playbook fires and completes its action automatically Full chain Repeat the brute-force test start to finish You can trace: attack → IDS/HIDS alert → SIEM dashboard → SOAR action, without manual steps in between

docs.title: Baseline already validated
docs.text: Step 3.9 proved a controlled Windows Application event can trigger a marker-file response through Wazuh and Shuffle, with a separate manual reversal. Positive conditions executed the downstream action; negative conditions skipped it. This is a SOAR plumbing baseline, not proof of brute-force detection, host containment, network isolation, or the full attack-to-SIEM-to-response chain. The OpenVAS baseline found one host and four informational results; authenticated vulnerability coverage remains open. See Shuffle evidence and integration record.

docs.title: Exit Criteria for Phase 4
docs.text:
• [ ] All 7 tests above pass
  • [ ] Any failures documented with root cause (e.g., "logs weren't reaching Splunk because the forwarder wasn't installed")

docs.title: PHASE 5 — Deployment / Go-Live
docs.text:
Goal: Move from "under construction" to "operational lab I use regularly."

October 21 status: preparing deployment readiness while Phase 4 tests and regression gates remain open. Successful startup and GUI access do not establish full operational acceptance. See latest activities and evidence.

  1. Create VMware snapshots of every VM once it's in a known-good state for rollback. Snapshots do not replace independent backups; validate recovery separately.
  2. Write yourself a one-page "power-on order" cheat sheet (pfSense first, then victims, then whichever SIEM/tool pod you're using that session) based on Section 1.3's pod strategy. Update: Pod A (pfSense, Windows victim, Wazuh) is now configured in VMware Workstation to AutoStart with the host — one less manual step each session, though it's still worth confirming all three came up cleanly after a host reboot before relying on the lab being "just on."
  3. Document credentials and IPs somewhere safe (a local password manager, not a plain text file on the desktop).
  4. Harden pfSense before considering the lab "live." During Phase 3 you likely loosened outbound rules on one or more zones so VMs could patch/update. Before go-live, walk back through every zone and tighten:
  5. Attacker zone: should only be able to reach the Corp zone (to simulate an external attacker) and, if you want Kali itself to stay patched, a narrow outbound-only allowance for updates — it should not be able to reach Management.
  6. Corp zone: should reach Management only on the specific ports your agents/tools need (e.g., Wazuh agent port, Suricata/log forwarding ports), not "any."
  7. Management zone: can stay permissive outbound since it's your own tooling, but should not be reachable from the Attacker zone at all.
  8. Remove any temporary "allow any outbound" rules you added per-VM during building/patching in Phase 3.
  9. Confirm: rerun the Phase 4 network isolation test after hardening to make sure tightening the rules didn't also break log forwarding or agent connectivity.

docs.title: Exit Criteria for Phase 5
docs.text:
• [ ] Snapshots taken of all VMs
  • [ ] Power-on cheat sheet written
  • [ ] Credentials stored securely
  • [ ] Temporary "build-phase" firewall rules removed and permanent hardened rules in place
  • [ ] Phase 4 isolation test re-run successfully after hardening

docs.title: PHASE 6 — Maintenance
docs.text: Goal: Keep the lab useful over time instead of it rotting after week one.

docs.title: Lab startup checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Select the smallest viable pod and check host available RAM and VM/host disk space before starting additional VMs. Include the DC when domain/DNS dependencies require it.
  • [ ] Confirm required services and fresh telemetry, not only console/GUI access. Check pfSense syslogd remains running; a green status at boot does not establish continued delivery.
  • [ ] For scanner sessions, inspect existing tasks/reports before starting another scan.
  • [ ] OpenVAS feed freshness gate: open Administration → Feed Status and record NVT, SCAP, CERT and GVMD_DATA versions/status. If stale or syncing, complete the feed maintenance below before a new assessment. Reviewing historical reports does not require a new feed import.
  • [ ] Verify endpoint scan readiness: domain profile, RemoteRegistry/Winmgmt service state, scanner-scoped firewall rules and credentials. Keep Defender enabled. See endpoint build guide.
  • [ ] Record readiness results and unresolved exceptions in the day's activity log. Power off unused pods after the task.

docs.title: OpenVAS feed-only maintenance
docs.text: Check feeds whenever OpenVAS is started for scanning, especially after lab downtime. Refresh when stale; do not blindly download feeds at every startup. Feed freshness is separate from Ubuntu host patching and scanner application-image updates. A host package upgrade does not refresh these feeds.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
1. Confirm no scans are running. Record existing feed versions, current container images and available disk/RAM. Preserve exported reports privately.
  2. Confirm a suitable recovery point exists. Feed imports alter shared feed volumes and databases; restarting an older image alone is not a complete rollback. Plan application-image/Compose changes separately, retaining local customizations and checking upstream compatibility.
  3. Keep the approved scanner pod running and unnecessary VMs off. Do not start a new assessment while feed import is incomplete.

docs.title: Download and load feed data
docs.text:
Run on the OpenVAS host, one command at a time. Proceed to the second only if the download succeeds:

sudo docker compose -f /home/seclabadmin/greenbone-ce/compose.yaml pull notus-data vulnerability-tests scap-data dfn-cert-data cert-bund-data report-formats data-objects

sudo docker compose -f /home/seclabadmin/greenbone-ce/compose.yaml up -d notus-data vulnerability-tests scap-data dfn-cert-data cert-bund-data report-formats data-objects

These commands select feed services; they do not intentionally pull the complete application stack. Running scanner/manager daemons automatically import the copied feed data. Completion of pull/up alone is not completion of synchronization. Import can take minutes to hours.

docs.title: Validation and acceptance
docs.text:
• [ ] Inspect container state and recent import logs:
sudo docker compose -f /home/seclabadmin/greenbone-ce/compose.yaml ps -a
sudo docker compose -f /home/seclabadmin/greenbone-ce/compose.yaml logs --since 30m --tail 100 ospd-openvas gvmd
  • [ ] Confirm relevant import completion, such as Finished loading VTs, Updating VTs in database ... done, Updating SCAP info succeeded, and Updating CERT info succeeded. Logs may rotate or imports may take longer than the shown window; absence in this sample alone is not failure.
  • [ ] Refresh Administration → Feed Status: record final versions and confirm no synchronization is still active and no stale status remains. Do not require a literal same-day feed timestamp if no newer upstream feed is available; document that exception.
  • [ ] Verify saved targets, credentials references, custom scan configuration and historical reports remain accessible. Never record credential secrets.
  • [ ] Only then permit a new scan. Feed refresh alone does not close the native WMI authentication-setting issue.

If import fails, capture logs and check resources; avoid repeated blind restarts. Do not delete volumes or run down -v. Restore a recovery point only under a deliberate rollback plan, accounting for reports/settings created since that point.

Source: Greenbone Community Containers feed synchronization workflow.

docs.title: Maintenance cadence
docs.text:
• Weekly: Power on your current pod, run one attack scenario end-to-end, confirm detection still works.
  • Monthly: Patch pfSense, Wazuh, and whichever SIEM you're actively using (staying current matters — this mirrors real patch management, which is itself something SOC analysts monitor for).
  • Ongoing: Add new attack scenarios (e.g., simulate ransomware behavior, phishing payloads, lateral movement) and confirm each is detected — this is what turns the lab from a one-time build into an actual skills portfolio.
  • Before interviews: Take screenshots of your dashboards, alerts, and SOAR playbooks — this lab is resume/portfolio material.

TLP:CLEAR

Report date: October 3, 2026 | Case: SOC-HUNT-2026-001 | Audience: lab management and decision makers

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: The hunt examined whether unauthorized use of legitimate administration tools, accounts, and persistence mechanisms was present in the SOC home lab, using behavior described in public Volt Typhoon guidance. No confirmed compromise was identified in the reviewed evidence, so the hypothesis was not supported; it was not conclusively disproved because earlier activity was incompletely recorded. The observed activity was consistent with recognized user actions, security-agent checks, and software maintenance, with one Defender validation issue requiring operational follow-up. The investigation repaired missing log delivery and incorrect firewall timestamps, enabled additional auditing, and disabled a broad firewall rule that overrode more specific rules. The remaining priorities are to finish network segmentation, validate the new auditing, and improve historical evidence coverage before treating future empty searches as assurance.

The detailed report contains the commands, searches, observed results, confidence levels, and evidence references. The scope was a home-lab assessment, not a forensic investigation of a confirmed intrusion or an assessment of real critical infrastructure.

docs.title: Objective and intelligence
docs.text:
Hypothesis H1: unauthorized actors may use valid accounts and built-in administration tools to perform discovery, establish persistence, or access credentials while blending into normal administration. Public CISA advisory AA24-038A informed the behaviors selected for review. That advisory describes living-off-the-land behavior and use of valid accounts; it does not make the presence of net.exe, PowerShell, or other tools an actor-specific indicator. This home lab is not asserted to be a Volt Typhoon target or a critical-infrastructure environment. CISA AA24-038A

Hypothesis H2: the lab's telemetry is sufficient to observe and distinguish those behaviors. H2 was initially disproved for several sources: process auditing was disabled, Splunk was unavailable for earlier events, the TCP receiver was absent, firewall pass logging was ineffective on the intended rule, and service/task auditing was disabled. The fixes improved current visibility, but end-to-end service/task event generation remains pending validation.

The operator executed commands on the VMs and supplied outputs. Analysis compared local Windows records, Wazuh alerts, Splunk exports, firewall logs, signatures, and user recognition of activity. The command log distinguishes commands visible in the record from reconstructed repeatable procedures. Commands reconstructed from described work are not represented as exact historical keystrokes. A successful TCP connection proves connectivity, not event ingestion. A process-name match identifies a candidate, not a compromise.

docs.title: Phase 1 Visibility baseline and process validation
docs.text:
WazuhSvc was running, but Windows Audit Process Creation initially showed No Auditing and the command-line audit registry value was absent. Success auditing and ProcessCreationIncludeCmdLine_Enabled=1 were enabled. A benign cmd.exe marker produced local Security 4688 record 42962 at September 24 19:30:42; Wazuh received it at 19:30:45.988−0600 under rule 67027, level 3. This verified local generation and manager detection, not complete forwarding history.

The original Splunk search did not locate the first marker. Subsequent tests labeled TEST_02 returned records 43496 and 43497 at 20:36:03 and 20:36:08. These are distinct process executions, not evidence of duplicate ingestion. Manager alert forwarding had no restrictive level filter, and a packet capture at the receiver showed datagrams. No filter change was needed merely because no explicit minimum level was present. Wazuh alerts are a subset of Windows event records, not a raw-event archive. Wazuh syslog output

The discovery test generated whoami /all, hostname, ipconfig /all, net user, and tasklist. Splunk returned records 43509, 43511, 43512, 43514 and 43515; net1.exe was a child of net.exe, while the other visible commands had PowerShell parents. Tasklist record 43513 existed locally at 20:40:44 and in Wazuh at 20:40:47.068 but was not located in Splunk. Repeated filtered tasklist executions arrived as records 43538 and 43539. The missing original record remains a collection anomaly; the investigation did not prove UDP truncation, packet loss, or an attacker action.

Process searches initially used a candidate-name list without extracting process_name after a login-query edit. The complete 4688 extraction and basename normalization corrected that query. A zero from the incomplete query was not a meaningful negative finding. Benign higher-risk-tool checks generated netsh interface portproxy show all (record 43612, 21:10:45) and sc query WazuhSvc (43613, 21:11:14). Both matched seclabadmin with PowerShell parents. Portproxy returned no entries in current configuration; the service query checked rather than changed Wazuh.

docs.title: Phase 2 Session and logon review
docs.text:
Local record 42807 identified September 24 19:26:15 session 0x7a169, local SOC-VICT-WIN10\seclabadmin, type 2, source 127.0.0.1, Negotiate. Wazuh rule 60118 recorded it at 19:26:18.877−0600. Splunk did not contain it; the operator confirmed Splunk started later. This is a receiver-availability limitation rather than a field-extraction explanation.

Four received type 2 records represented later sessions: 43484/43485 at September 24 20:35:48, and 40321/40322 at September 20 01:16:10. All concerned seclabadmin and localhost. The preserved CSV reports raw lengths 4,026–4,028 characters and complete endings. Their session IDs differ from 0x7a169, so they cannot be substituted as the discovery session's initial logon.

An earlier local type 3 event, record 42761 at September 24 19:25:54, reported ANONYMOUS LOGON, SID S-1-5-7, session 0x2b3bc, NtLmSsp, and absent IP/workstation/process information. A bounded correlation search returned only that original event. Process auditing had not yet been enabled, limiting correlation. The NTLM V1 text for anonymous logon does not alone prove NTLMv1 credential negotiation. The event is unexplained, not classified as malicious. Microsoft anonymous NTLM guidance

The October 3 direct-feed export contained 18 events 4624 and one 4648. Sixteen 4624 records were SYSTEM type 5 service logons initiated by services.exe. Two type 2 records at 02:04:34.508 were linked seclabadmin sessions (0x1B0AC16, 0x1B0AB73) from 127.0.0.1 through svchost.exe. The simultaneous 4648 used that local account against localhost through the same process PID 0x6c4. The operator confirmed signing in/unlocking at that time. No type 3 or type 10 occurred in that 19-record export; this is not a claim about all host history.

docs.title: Phase 3 Current persistence and binary checks
docs.text:
The initial non-Microsoft task inventory contained Brave and Edge update tasks, OneDrive reporting/update/startup tasks, and Firefox update/default-browser tasks. The operator recognized the Security Admin account. BraveUpdate, MicrosoftEdgeUpdate, Firefox and default-browser-agent signatures were valid with expected publishers. OneDrive updater copies for seclabadmin and Security Admin and the seclabadmin OneDriveLauncher signature were valid Microsoft signatures. No OneDrive directory under the SplunkForwarder service profile was expected evidence of compromise.

The inventory also contained an Administrator SID−500 OneDrive task, but no corresponding Administrator profile was returned by the profile enumeration. That task was not verified or removed. Its stale-task explanation is a possibility, not a finding of legitimacy.

Microsoft task candidates used rundll32, PowerShell and dsregcmd with maintenance-shaped arguments. The SMB client/server uninstall tasks referenced DisableUnusedSmb1.ps1; that script's current Microsoft Windows signature was valid. The -ExecutionPolicy Unrestricted and hidden-window arguments were evaluated in context rather than treated as proof of malicious PowerShell. Other task DLLs, definitions, owners and permissions were not all verified.

The service inventory showed expected lab/browser/Defender/VMware programs and running Wazuh and SplunkForwarder services. The earlier seven-day System 7045 review returned KslD driver installation (September 19, record 3967), VMware SVGA Helper (September 20, 4106), and VMware Snapshot Provider (4115). KslD had a valid Microsoft Windows signature and product Microsoft Malware Protection. The operator recognized the VMware installation timing. Not every service binary was signature-verified. The later October 3 rolling seven-day 7045 query returned no entries; that narrower date range no longer included the September 19–20 installations.

docs.title: Phase 4 Live connections and firewall telemetry
docs.text:
Live connection ownership identified MpDefenderCoreService PID 3300 → 52.123.248.83:443, svchost PID 3552 → 20.59.87.225:443, and wazuh-agent PID 3520 → 10.10.10.11:1514. CIM service mapping associated the first two with MDCoreSvc and WpnService. Process ownership supported expected operational context, but destination hostnames, payloads and reputation were not independently validated.

Splunk's non-Wazuh source inventory initially contained only 25 pfSense DHCP entries, renewing WAN address 10.10.40.101 via observed DHCP server 10.10.40.110 in five cycles. Remote syslog destinations and Firewall Events selection were configured, but local firewall results showed only blocked IPv6 multicast DNS. Protocol UDP in that list did not imply the victim generated only UDP traffic: the HTTPS tests were TCP and initially unlogged.

Logging on the first Corporate allow rule remained checked, yet fresh successful connections to 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1 did not match it. The loaded ruleset showed quick floating rule @94 tracker 1786962198, pass IPv4 any-to-any, no logging at that stage. It had substantial packet/state counters, while the later Corporate rule's counters were zero. This explained why enabling logging on the later rule did not produce the test event. Floating quick rules are processed before interface rules. Netgate floating rules

Logging was temporarily enabled on the floating rule to validate the path. A test to 1.1.1.1:80 produced Corporate and WAN-side entries. WAN records had translated source 10.10.40.101; a Splunk query requiring 10.10.20.20 intentionally omitted those rows. Three endpoint rows versus six local interface rows did not prove ingestion loss. A timestamp mismatch was then isolated with the SOC_TIME_TEST syslog marker.

The pfSense timezone was changed from fixed MST to America/Denver. Shell time read MDT−0600, and a system logger marker matched Splunk, while filterlog PID 5400 still emitted timestamps an hour behind. Calling filter_pflog_start(true) returned the requested echo but did not replace PID 5400. That echo was insufficient restart validation. After the operator rebooted pfSense, a fresh event at 20:57:48 showed filterlog PID 52199; embedded time, Splunk _time, and receipt time all agreed. Earlier records retained their original discrepancy.

The operator confirmed management access at 10.10.10.5 before disabling the broad floating rule, since administration usually used WAN DHCP address 10.10.40.101 from host 10.10.40.1. The rule was disabled, saved and applied. At September 25 21:05:42, a fresh Corporate connection from 10.10.20.20:54926 to 1.0.0.1:80 matched tracker 1786792812, the temporary Corporate internet rule. Existing states were not globally cleared. The rule transition is verified for this new connection, not retroactively for every existing flow. Corporate still permits any destination; segmentation remains incomplete.

Some blocked records contained finish/reset flags after the reboot; these are not sufficient to infer attempted compromise or a broad egress policy change.

Current victim connections showed PID 3596 splunkd with 8089 Established and 9997 SynSent. Server ss showed no 9997 listener, and btool inputs list splunktcp://9997 --debug returned no receiver stanza. The receiver was created through Splunk Web. An initial 15-minute source inventory returned 98 direct events: performance metrics plus Application and System. Security collection was enabled (disabled=0, current_only=0, start_from=oldest, index default), and a broader subsequent search returned 845 Security events in main. The suggestion that index=default implied an internal destination was incorrect and was corrected. These snapshots were taken at different times and cannot prove whether elapsed ingestion, the broader time window, or another condition caused the earlier absence. Security receipt in main is directly verified.

The next event inventory returned 620 process events and 15 logons; later exports contained 626 and 18 respectively, because collection continued. Differences between successive snapshots are not treated as duplicates or anomalies. Collection success does not prove all historic records were backfilled; the available October 3 process export covers only the stated shorter span.

docs.title: Phase 6 Direct Security process review
docs.text:
All 626 records in the process export contained command lines. Frequent processes included conhost (112), .NET ngen (126 across architectures), auditpol (54), backgroundTaskHost (36), Splunk helper processes, browser updaters, and maintenance utilities. Seventeen ordinary PowerShell events had wazuh-agent.exe as parent and exported security policy before selecting password or lockout settings. Auditpol commands used /get; WMIC queried the Guest account's disabled status; net user enumerated accounts; registry commands queried legal notice values. That combination supports Wazuh configuration-assessment context rather than unauthorized policy changes.

VMware vmtoolsd launched resume-vm-default.bat through cmd, followed by ipconfig /renew. Rundll32 arguments referenced previously inventoried maintenance tasks. Wevtutil installed/uninstalled application event manifests rather than clearing Security logs. The Splunk btool command matched the operator's check. OneDrive and browser installer activity was consistent with update activity, but the process names and paths alone did not authenticate every binary. No LSASS/NTDS dumping, encoded PowerShell download, malicious scheduled-task creation, log clearing, or portproxy addition was demonstrated in these records. This is a bounded assessment of the actual export.

docs.title: Phase 7 Defender integrity candidate
docs.text:
Security 5038 record 47412 at October 3 01:58:47.320 flagged DefenderSessionHelper.exe under platform 4.18.26080.4-0. The current Authenticode signature was Valid, publisher Microsoft Windows. Code Integrity Operational 3004 and 3089 had the same ActivityID {c6bc20a0-4c8c-0000-0730-bfc68c4cdd01}, process/thread 3508/10532, and timestamps differing by microseconds. Event 3004 identified MsMpEng.exe as requesting process, RequestedSigningLevel 7, SecureRequired 0x80000018. Event 3089 reported one signature, Windows publisher, Windows Production PCA 2023 issuer, ValidatedSigningLevel 12 and VerificationError 12.

Microsoft defines verification error 12 as not valid for PPL. The correlated result supports a protected-process signature requirement failure even though ordinary current Authenticode verification succeeded. The generic 5038/3004 wording was refined using the correlated details; file modification was not proven. Classification: Defender signing/compatibility candidate, with underlying cause and recurrence unresolved. Do not disable protection, exclude the file, or lower signing policy on this evidence. Microsoft event tags

The hash field was supplied by Code Integrity and not recomputed as a whole-file hash. Certificate validity dates in the event spanned April 30, 2026 through April 29, 2027; the observation fell within those dates, but expiration alone is not the pertinent reported error.

docs.title: Phase 8 Service and scheduled task history
docs.text:
The direct Security search for 4697, 4698, 4702 and 1102 returned no results. Auditpol then showed Security System Extension and Other Object Access Events set to No Auditing. Therefore the negative service/task results were not evidence of absence. Both subcategories were enabled for Success and the effective output verified. The policy check did not test Security-log clearing coverage; the 1102 empty result is only an observed query result.

The latest local System 7045 seven-day query returned no entries with errors suppressed. A channel-access or collection failure was not independently excluded by that empty output; confidence is limited accordingly. Task Scheduler Operational was enabled with RecordCount 17,448 and LastWriteTime October 3 02:37:19 at inspection. A seven-day export for IDs 106, 140 and 141 returned 212 events, all parsed successfully, across 20 unique task paths.

There were 210 updates, one deletion and one registration. The deletion and registration both concerned the same seclabadmin SID−1002 OneDrive Standalone Update task at October 3 01:58:24. This aligns with OneDriveSetup execution in the process export. UpdateOrchestrator's Schedule Work, Schedule Wake To Work and Schedule Maintenance Work contributed 56 updates each; the other changes concerned Group Policy, Defender, .NET NGEN, Device Information, Edge, OneDrive, Flighting, PushToInstall and WindowsUpdate RUXIM. The names, user contexts and timing support maintenance, but history messages contain no task actions/XML and do not authenticate all task content. No unexplained task name was identified. Full current definitions and security descriptors remain outside this final history review.

docs.title: Detection proposals
docs.text: The command appendix provides repeatable triage searches and a harmless task-validation procedure. Proposed analytics should cover sensitive process commands, service/task creation, log clearing, unexpected remote logons, collection failures and recurring Code Integrity failures. Require command arguments, parents, account context and sequence correlation rather than standalone executable-name alerts. Establish a narrow baseline for Wazuh assessment checks and Splunk helper processes; do not exclude all PowerShell or all Microsoft-signed files. No proposed rule has been deployed or regression-tested in this report.

docs.title: What worked
docs.text: Local-to-manager-to-Splunk record comparison exposed source and forwarding gaps. Effective ruleset counters identified the actual matched firewall rule. Fresh connections distinguished new rules from retained state. Index receipt time and a labeled logger marker separated clock versus logging-process behavior. Direct Security events provided command lines and session details that the alert subset could miss. Operator recognition helped resolve the local sign-in without asserting attribution.

docs.title: What needs improvement
docs.text: Verify collection before interpreting negative searches. Separate local clock, embedded logger timestamp, event time and ingestion time. Treat an echo saying restart requested as an attempt, not successful restart evidence. The report corrects the erroneous internal-index suggestion and retains the original snapshot limitations. Use single commands or assigned result variables to avoid merged paste pipelines; export large outputs to files instead of truncating chat. Audit settings must be validated with harmless generated events and policy persistence checks. Current snapshots and valid signatures cannot exclude past tampering or all persistence.

docs.title: Conclusion and closure criteria
docs.text: H1 remains unproven: no confirmed malicious activity or Volt Typhoon attribution was established. This hunt pass is closed for the reviewed evidence, while remediation and coverage actions remain open. There is no empirical attack progression from reconnaissance to actions on objectives to reconstruct; the report instead documents checks at each phase and their negative or provisional findings. Reopen for an unexplained task/service action, unrecognized remote logon, credential-dumping behavior, process-correlated suspicious destination, repeated integrity failure with additional evidence, or material collection gap.
